Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

Assume countable choice. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the wavelet or trigonometric basis from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. Let $Z_{lk}$ be mutually independent real random variables with density $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Define the formal white-noise coefficient sequence $W=(Z_{lk})$. For every $\delta>1/2$, this sequence is almost surely an element of $H(\delta)$ and is a Borel Gaussian random element there. Its law $N$ is a Borel probability on $H(\delta)$. For an infinite-dimensional basis, white noise is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued random element. Here Gaussian means that each continuous real linear functional has a centered law $N(0,v)$ in the density convention of [[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series]]; in particular, for $L(c)=\sum_jd_jc_j$ its variance is $\sum_jd_j^2$ whenever this pairing is continuous on $H(\delta)$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let
$f_n : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then the functions

$$\sup_n f_n,\qquad \inf_n f_n,\qquad \limsup_n f_n,\qquad \liminf_n f_n$$

are measurable. The set

$$\{\, x : \lim_n f_n(x) \text{ exists in } \overline{\mathbb{R}} \,\}$$

is measurable. In particular, if $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then
$\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $N$ let $V_N=\operatorname{span}\{u_j:j\in J,\ j\le N\}$ and let $P_Ng=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$. Orthonormality gives $g-P_Ng\perp V_N$. For any $v\in H$, expanding the inner product of $v=P_Nv+(v-P_Nv)$ gives $\|v\|^2=\|P_Nv\|^2+\|v-P_Nv\|^2$, so $\|P_Nv\|\le\|v\|$. Given $\eta>0$, density of the finite span in [F2] gives $w\in V_M$ with $\|g-w\|<\eta$; for $N\ge M$, $P_Nw=w$, so $\|g-P_Ng\|\le\|g-w\|+\|P_N(w-g)\|\le2\|g-w\|<2\eta$. Thus $P_Ng\to g$ in norm, with the finite-basis case eventually equal to $g$.

For distinct indices $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, [F1] gives independent standard-normal variables $Z(u_{j_1}),\ldots,Z(u_{j_m})$. Since $\epsilon>0$, the affine map $z\mapsto\mu_{j_r}+\epsilon z$ and its inverse are continuous, so $Y_x(u_{j_r})$ and its noise coordinate generate the same sigma-algebra; independence therefore transfers. The affine-image definition of $N$ gives each law $N(\mu_{j_r},\epsilon^2)$.

Put $c_j=\langle g,u_j\rangle_H$. The linearity clause in [F1] applied to the finite sum defining $P_Ng$ gives $Z(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}c_jZ(u_j)$; linearity of the inner product gives $\langle Kx,P_Ng\rangle_H=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}c_j\mu_j$. Combining these identities yields $Y_x(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}c_jY_x(u_j)$.

In the carrier case covered by [F4]–[F5], [F1] supplies independent coordinates with the common standard-normal density and [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F5]. Hence [F5] makes the noise coefficient sequence a Borel Gaussian random element of $H(\delta)$; [F4] puts each deterministic signal $Kx$ in the same space. Their sum $Kx+\epsilon W$ is therefore an $H(\delta)$-valued Borel random element, and every continuous linear functional of it is a translate and positive rescaling of the corresponding centered Gaussian functional.

In the infinite-dimensional function-space case, if $Kx+\epsilon W$ were an $H$-valued sample on an event of probability one, then $W=((Kx+\epsilon W)-Kx)/\epsilon$ would also be $H$-valued there, since $Kx\in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. This contradicts [F5], so the sample is not $H$-valued.

With $r_N=g-P_Ng$, linearity gives $Y_x(g)-Y_x(P_Ng)=\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(r_N)$. Centering and the covariance identity in [F1] give $\mathbb E Z(r_N)=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z(r_N)^2]=\|r_N\|_H^2$; expanding the square therefore shows that the squared mean-square error is $|\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H|^2+\epsilon^2\|r_N\|_H^2$. By [F3] and step 1.1, both terms tend to zero, proving the asserted mean-square reconstruction. For any finite list of test vectors, the sum of their finitely many squared errors also tends to zero, so the coordinate reconstructions converge jointly in product mean square.

By step 1.1, for each $g$ and $k\ge1$ the set of integers $N\ge k$ with $\|g-P_Ng\|_H\le2^{-k}$ is nonempty. Its least element $N_k(g)$ is uniquely defined, with no choice and no dependence on $x$, $Kx$ or the observations. For fixed $g,k$, $a_{g,k}$ is a finite linear combination of coordinate evaluations on $\mathbb R^J$, hence is measurable. By [F8], its limsup and liminf are measurable; their equality set, intersected with the set where their common value is finite, is the measurable real-convergence set $A_g$. Defining $T(z)(g)$ to equal that limit on $A_g$ and zero on its complement is measurable: for a Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage is $A_g\cap\{\limsup_k a_{g,k}\in B\}$, together with $A_g^c$ if $0\in B$. Thus every evaluation of $T$ is measurable, which makes $T$ measurable into $\mathcal C_H$. Each coordinate of $S$ is a field evaluation, so $S$ is measurable into $\mathcal C_J$ as well.

Fix $x$ and $g$. By steps 1.3 and 2.1, the real random variable $D_k=a_{g,k}(S(Y_x))-Y_x(g)$ satisfies $\mathbb E|D_k|^2\le(\|Kx\|_H^2+\epsilon^2)4^{-k}$. For every positive integer $r$, [F6] applied to $|D_k|^2$ at threshold $r^{-2}$ gives $\mathbb P\{|D_k|\ge1/r\}\le r^2(\|Kx\|_H^2+\epsilon^2)4^{-k}$. The right-hand side is summable in $k$, so [F7] makes $|D_k|<1/r$ eventually almost surely for each $r$. The union over $r\ge1$ of these null exceptional events is null: disjointifying the union and using countable additivity bounds its probability by the sum of zeros. Off that union $D_k\to0$, proving $T(S(Y_x))(g)=Y_x(g)$ almost surely. All limits here concern the explicitly specified representatives at a fixed $x,g$; the $L^2$ equalities used to compute the error hold almost surely and therefore give exactly the same second moments.

The coordinate law $Q_x=S_*P_x$ and the reconstructed law $T_*Q_x$ are probability measures by [F10]; they use only pushforwards of the given process, with no new product-existence assumption. For any finite list $g_1,\ldots,g_n$, intersect the finitely many probability-one events in step 3.1. On that intersection the reconstructed and original evaluation vectors agree, so $T_*Q_x$ and $P_x$ agree on every finite cylinder $\{y:(y(g_1),\ldots,y(g_n))\in B\}$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. These cylinders form a generating pi-system for $\mathcal C_H$, and both measures have total mass one, so [F9] gives $T_*Q_x=P_x$ on $\mathcal C_H$. This proves equality of laws without any uncountable intersection of probability-one events.

For every basis index $j$, $N_k(u_j)\ge k\ge j$ once $k\ge j$, so orthonormality gives $a_{u_j,k}(z)=z_j$ then, for every $z\in\mathbb R^J$. Consequently $T(z)(u_j)=z_j$ and $S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R^J}$ everywhere. If $J=\varnothing$, completeness forces $H=\{0\}$, every sum defining $a_{0,k}$ is zero, and $T$ returns the zero field; linearity gives $Y_x(0)=0$ almost surely. If $J$ is nonempty and finite, $P_N=I$ after its last index, so the same construction reduces to the finite linear reconstruction and all preceding arguments apply. Thus the maps in the Statement establish both sampling-law identities in every allowed dimension. The least-index construction spends no choice principle; the only countable-choice use remains step 1.4.

boundaries.evidence: For J empty, H={0}; the coefficient space is a singleton and T returns the zero field. Step 5.1 proves the sampling-law identities.
For Kx=0, step 1.2 gives centered coordinate laws; the bound in step 3.1 and both reconstruction-law identities still hold.
For a one-dimensional finite basis, P_N=I after its only index; step 5.1 gives the finite measurable reconstruction.
For zero residual g-P_Ng, step 2.1 gives zero mean-square error. Step 5.1 handles exact basis-coordinate reconstruction.
The Statement requires epsilon>0. Its optional negative-Sobolev clause and step 1.4 require delta>1/2 and the specified basis; no endpoint carrier claim is made.
Least N>=k with residual <=2^-k exists by step 1.1 and is uniquely selected in step 2.2. The fixed-basis cylinder clause is choice-free; countable choice is used only in step 1.4.
S is measurable by step 2.2 and S_*P_x=Q_x by definition; step 4.1 identifies the coordinate pushforward probability law.
Steps 2.2, 3.1 and 4.1 prove measurable parameter-independent T and T_*Q_x=P_x on the cylinder sigma-algebra; step 5.1 proves S composed with T is identity everywhere.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space with a fixed complete orthonormal basis $(u_j)$, indexed by $J=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for $m\in\mathbb N_0$ or by $J=\mathbb N_{>0}$; the empty basis covers $H=\{0\}$. Let $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ be the isonormal white-noise experiment with $\epsilon>0$, and write $\mu_j=\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_H$. For every parameter $x$ and every basis index $j$, the observations $Y_x(u_j)$ are independent and have laws $N(\mu_j,\epsilon^2)$, where $N$ is the scalar normal law defined in the experiment.

For $g\in H$, set $P_Ng=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$, with $P_N=I$ once all vectors of a finite basis have been included. Then

$$Y_x(g)=L^2(\mathbb P)\text{-}\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_HY_x(u_j).$$

Thus every finite collection of observation functionals is reconstructed from the coefficient sequence in mean square. This does not assert almost-sure convergence of the full sequence of partial sums, a simultaneous path identity for all test vectors, or an $H$-valued observation.

More precisely, let $\mathcal C_H$ be the cylinder sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^H$, let $\mathcal C_J$ be the sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^J$ generated by its coordinate evaluations, and let $P_x$ be the field sampling law. Define $S:\mathbb R^H\to\mathbb R^J$ by $S(y)_j=y(u_j)$ and $Q_x=S_*P_x$, where a pushforward is $S_*P_x(B)=P_x(S^{-1}(B))$. $$S_*P_x=Q_x,\qquad T_*Q_x=P_x,\qquad S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R^J}.$$

These parameter-independent maps give equivalence of the field cylinder experiment and its coefficient experiment. One such map is the following. For $k\ge1$ and $g\in H$, let $N_k(g)$ be the least integer $N\ge k$ with $\|g-P_Ng\|_H\le2^{-k}$ and put

$$a_{g,k}(z)=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N_k(g)}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hz_j,\qquad T(z)(g)=\begin{cases}\lim_{k\to\infty}a_{g,k}(z),&\text{if the limit exists in }\mathbb R,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

The exceptional event may depend on $x$ and on that list; no intersection over all $g\in H$ is asserted. In dimension zero the coefficient space is a singleton and $T$ returns the field with value zero at $g=0$.

If $H=L^2([0,1])$ and the basis is one of the wavelet or trigonometric bases used to define the negative Sobolev carrier $H(\delta)$, then under countable choice and for $\delta>1/2$ the same coordinate sequence is a Borel Gaussian random element in $H(\delta)$ with mean coefficients $Kx$ and noise level $\epsilon$. In infinite dimension it is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued sample.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\Theta\subseteq X$ be a nonempty parameter set, let $K:X\to H$ be a signal map, and let $\epsilon>0$. For $x\in\Theta$ and $g\in H$, define the observation functional

$$Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g).$$

The associated statistical inverse experiment has sample space $\mathbb R^H$ with the cylinder sigma-algebra generated by the evaluation maps $y\mapsto y(g)$, and its sampling law $P_x$ is the law of the random function $g\mapsto Y_x(g)$. Each sample is indexed by test functionals on $H$; it is not asserted to be a vector in $H$ or to have a continuous path. If $H=\{0\}$, linearity forces $Z(0)=0$ and the experiment is deterministic.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space with a fixed complete orthonormal basis $(u_j)$, indexed by $J=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ for $m\in\mathbb N_0$ or by $J=\mathbb N_{>0}$; the empty basis covers $H=\{0\}$. Let $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ be the isonormal white-noise experiment with $\epsilon>0$, and write $\mu_j=\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_H$. For every parameter $x$ and every basis index $j$, the observations $Y_x(u_j)$ are independent and have laws $N(\mu_j,\epsilon^2)$, where $N$ is the scalar normal law defined in the experiment.

For $g\in H$, set $P_Ng=\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$, with $P_N=I$ once all vectors of a finite basis have been included. Then

$$Y_x(g)=L^2(\mathbb P)\text{-}\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j\in J,\ j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_HY_x(u_j).$$

Thus every finite collection of observation functionals is reconstructed from the coefficient sequence in mean square. This does not assert almost-sure convergence of the full sequence of partial sums, a simultaneous path identity for all test vectors, or an $H$-valued observation.

There is a measurable map $T:(\mathbb R^J,\mathcal C_J)\to(\mathbb R^H,\mathcal C_H)$, depending only on the indexed basis, such that for every parameter $x$,

In dimension zero the coefficient space is a singleton and $T$ returns the field with value zero at $g=0$.

derivations.claim: Since $g=P_Ng+r_N$ and the process is linear by [F1], $Y_x(g)=Y_x(P_Ng)+Y_x(r_N)$. Applying [F2] to $P_Ng$, whose later finite projections equal $P_Ng$, gives $Y_x(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_HY_x(u_j)$; the definition gives $Y_x(r_N)=\langle h,r_N\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(r_N)$. This proves the displayed decomposition.

The residual $r_N$ is orthogonal to $u_1,\ldots,u_N$. If $r_N\ne0$, adjoining $r_N/\|r_N\|_H$ to these vectors gives a finite orthonormal tuple, so [F1] makes $Z(r_N/\|r_N\|_H)$ independent of the first $N$ coordinate noises; linearity gives $Z(r_N)=\|r_N\|_H Z(r_N/\|r_N\|_H)$ as an equality of its almost-sure equivalence classes. Since $\epsilon>0$, this noise and the tail observation are invertible affine functions of one another, so the tail observation is independent of the first $N$ coordinates. The covariance identity gives its variance $\epsilon^2\|r_N\|_H^2$ and its mean is $\langle h,r_N\rangle_H$. If $r_N=0$, both are zero.
